1:
Chrysostom alone reconstructs the objection Paul is fending off. It was likely, he says, that they would answer: if we were putting forward the opinions of Plato or Pythagoras you might well write at such length against us, but if we announce the things of the Spirit, why toss up and down the wisdom that is from without? The reply is that even in spiritual things they are learners and hindmost. Chrysostom notices the verb too: he said not I did not speak, lest it seem to proceed from grudging, but could not.

On the milk and the meat they agree, and divide over what follows from it. Barnes takes milk for the elementary doctrines, the new birth, repentance and faith, and meat for the more sublime, noting the same figure in the Epistle to the Hebrews; Gill adds that the Jews were themselves used to compare the law to milk, and Wesley draws the rule that every preacher should suit his doctrine to his hearers. Calvin raises the question that rule provokes — whether Paul transformed Christ to suit the diversity of his hearers — and answers that it refers to the manner and form of his instruction, not to the substance of the doctrine, the same truth being administered to both but suited to their capacity. Robertson works on the grammar instead: since the verb properly means to give drink, joining it to solid food is a zeugma, and the word rendered meat means not flesh as against bread but all solid food whatever.

What carnal means is the disputed point, and Robertson alone has the apparatus for it. The form at the first verse denotes the material of flesh, as in the fleshen tablets of the heart, while the form at the third means fitted for the flesh, of one who lives by it; both sorts of men are made of flesh, but the spiritual ought not to be fleshly. Gill guards the same ground without the Greek: the Syriac reads ye are in the flesh, a phrase Paul elsewhere uses of the unregenerate, but that is not his meaning here, only that carnality still prevailed among them. Barnes agrees that they are the friends of God in the main, yet so far as they are engaged in strife show themselves governed by the principles of the men of this world. Calvin puts it darkly. So long as natural corruption prevails it so possesses the mind that the wisdom of God finds no admittance; and though some sparks of piety were emitted among the Corinthians they were kept under by being choked, from which he draws that whoever would profit in the Lord's school must first renounce his own judgment and will.

Clarke sorts the three faults into thought, word and deed: envying is the state of their souls, who had inward grudgings; strife belongs to their words, each contending whose party was best; divisions are what came of it. Wesley has the same triad exactly. Ellicott marks the hinge instead. Hitherto ye were not able is better read for ye were not yet able: to this point the Apostle has been describing the condition in which he found them at his coming, so that he blames them not for having needed milk then but for needing it still. Henry supplies the moral: they had received the first principles without growing up to maturity in them, and were nevertheless very proud of their knowledge — it being but too common for persons of very moderate understanding to have a great measure of self-conceit. Calvin traces that conceit to their trade: in mercantile minds like theirs too much confidence and arrogance was still lingering, so that they embraced the simplicity of the gospel only with difficulty and were the readier to hear teachers subtle and showy but destitute of the Spirit.
4:
Why these two names and no others is answered three ways. Ellicott says only two factions are named, as types of the rest: the factious spirit was the same in all, but the difference between teaching the higher wisdom and the simpler truths was best illustrated by these two, and choosing those who called themselves by the Apostle's own name showed that no personal jealousy was at work. Wesley puts it as generosity, that Paul named himself and Apollos to show he would condemn any division even in his own favour, or the dearest friend he had, since the Spirit of God allows no party zeal. Calvin says he is personating the Corinthians so the description may have more force: they did not declare any such thing in express words, but he reproves the dispositions they were given up to, and where such ambition prevails the gospel has little or no success. Clarke adds the awkward fact underneath: Paul and Apollos held the same creed, with not the slightest difference between them, so that what captivated the people must have been something in the outward manner — Apollos being probably the more eloquent — which is itself the proof of carnality. Robertson notes that the clause is an indefinite temporal one with the subjunctive of repetition, each instance a fresh case in point, and that men here means mere human creatures, acting like the flesh and not like the Spirit. It was a home-thrust.

The answer given to the question is that the men are functions and not founders. Robertson observes that Paul does not ask who but what, using the neuter, and that the word rendered ministers means servants and nothing more — the technical sense of deacon comes later — so that no minister has any basis for pride. Henry states the danger plainly: they were but ministers, mere instruments used by the God of all grace, and some at Corinth had made more of them, as if they were lords of their faith; we should take care not to deify ministers, nor put them in the place of God. Gill asks the same in a row of questions — whether they were more than men, what authority they had, whether they were authors of a new religion or founders of a sect to go by their names. Barnes makes the inference: God is the fountain of all their blessings, and whoever was the instrument by whom they believed, it is improper to regard him as in any sense that fountain. Clarke turns even the differences between ministers back on God, whose judgment being infallible the distribution of talents must be right.

On the planting and the watering the same lesson is drawn from four directions. Calvin unfolds the similitude: the earth needs ploughing and sowing and other culture, but after all this is carefully done the husbandman's labour would be of no avail did not the Lord act from heaven, so that the diligence is not in vain and yet the fruit comes only by his blessing. Clarke says the same of both worlds at once, that it is neither the sower nor the waterer who produces the strange and inexplicable multiplication of the grain. Ellicott anchors the figure in the history: Paul as founder and Apollos as later instructor agrees exactly with what is told of Apollos coming to Corinth after him, taught by Aquila and Priscilla at Ephesus, and helping much those who had already believed. Robertson finds the whole argument in the tenses: planted and watered are aorists, single completed acts, but gave the increase is an imperfect, the continuous blessing of God on the work of both — reports of revivals sometimes give the glory to the evangelist; Paul gives it all to God.
7:
That the planter and waterer are nothing has to be kept from proving too much, and Barnes does the keeping. Take it comparatively, he says: they are nothing in comparison with God, but their agency is indispensable all the same. God could make a seed grow unplanted, but he does not; if the farmer does not plant, God will not make the grain grow. Ellicott reaches the same limit by the word, glossing any thing as anything worth mentioning. Robertson lets the logic stand unsoftened — God is the whole and we are not anything — applying the same neuter Paul used in asking not who but what these men were. Clarke turns it into a doxology, the seed God's, the ground God's, the labourers God's and the produce all from himself; Wesley reduces it to a line, that without him neither planting nor watering avails. Calvin alone warns that the depreciation must be read against Paul's other manner of speaking of ministers, since elsewhere he views one as set apart by the Lord to regenerate souls and nourish them.

In what sense the two are one is then divided out. Gill lists first the ways they are not: different men in different offices, Paul an apostle and Apollos only a preacher, unequal in gifts and usefulness; then the ways they are, having one commission, one gospel, one aim, and one affection for each other. Barnes numbers it a unity of end — the employments do not clash but tend to one result, and it is not as if one planted and the other were pulling up — each being as necessary as the other. Robertson notes that one here is again the neuter, and that if no one planted the watering would be useless and if no one watered the planting would come to naught — as the dreadful drought of the year he was writing in testified. Calvin puts it against the parties: the teachers are so linked that their connection allows no separation, since all have one end in view and serve one Lord.

Against that unity every one of them sets the individuality of the reward. Ellicott insists on the conjunction — the Apostle says but, not and as our version has it — so that each shall receive his own reward from God and not from man: there is an individuality as well as a unity in the ministry, which men will not notice but the great Master will. Clarke states the measure: God rewards his servants not according to the success of their labour, which depends on himself, but according to the quantum of faithful labour bestowed. Wesley says it as plainly: he who labours much though with small success shall have a great reward.

The last phrase divides them four ways. Barnes sets out both significations without forcing either: that they are co-workers with God, as a farmer co-operates with him in doing that without which no harvest would come, or else that they are workers belonging to God. Clarke argues for the second, rendering it with Bishop Pearce fellow labourers of God, since the preposition may join the teachers to one another rather than to God. Robertson takes the first boldly: the old word has a new dignity here, God being the major partner in each life who nevertheless lets us work with him. Calvin takes it the same way and makes it the commendation of the ministry: God, who could accomplish the whole himself, calls puny mortals to be as it were his coadjutors. Wesley declines to choose, keeping both: God's labourers, and fellow labourers with each other. Ellicott stands outside the quarrel and counts: three times the name of God is repeated with emphasis, and the image alters from agriculture to architecture because the second can be amplified further — such abrupt changes being characteristic of the Apostle.
10:
Calling himself a wise masterbuilder needs an excuse, and everyone notices that Paul supplies it first. Ellicott says he begins with the grace of God so as not to indulge in self-laudation but merely point out what God gave him grace to do; Gill adds that the phrase for masterbuilder is the Septuagint's. Henry turns the premise into a warning: spiritual pride is abominable, being the use of God's greatest favours to feed our own vanity and make idols of ourselves. Robertson and Calvin ask instead why the self-praise was necessary, and answer alike. Robertson says Paul does not shirk his share in the work at Corinth with all its sad outcome; he absolves Apollos and denies that he is himself to blame, and in doing so must praise himself, because those who fomented the trouble had blamed him directly. It is not always wise for a preacher to defend himself, but it is sometimes necessary. Calvin has him declaring his fidelity fearlessly against the calumnies of the wicked and the pride of the Corinthians alike: the more they lowered him, the higher he raises himself, as from a pulpit of vast height. Clarke divides the credit again: the design is God's, but the execution was entrusted chiefly to Paul as the architect God used to lay the foundation.

On the foundation itself there is no dispute, only different ways of fencing it. Robertson finds the point in the gender: the word for other is masculine and not neuter, because Paul has the person of Christ in mind, so that there is no room beside Jesus for a second Saviour of any name. Gill lists what men attempt instead — fleshly privilege, carnal descent, religious education, outward profession, a man's own righteousness, the absolute mercy of God — all sandy. Wesley answers who laid it by layers: in the counsels of divine wisdom, in the promises and prophecies of the older Scriptures, and in the apostles' preaching. Calvin makes it two-part: Christ is the only foundation, and the Corinthians were rightly founded on him through Paul's preaching, from which they could not draw back without forsaking Christ. Clarke and Henry both put the danger where the argument is going — the fear is not of another foundation but of a bad superstructure raised on a good one.

What the six materials stand for is the one real disagreement. Clarke, Wesley and Calvin read them as doctrines. Wesley makes it three that will bear the fire and three that will not, the latter all of human invention; Clarke names the false ones then current at Corinth, that there was to be no resurrection of the body and that a man might on his father's death lawfully marry his stepmother; Calvin says it were as absurd to raise vile materials on a foundation of gold as it is criminal to bury Christ under a mass of strange doctrines. Ellicott refuses the whole procedure. Many ingenious attempts have been made, he says, to apply the imagery in detail, but it is best taken broadly, as permanent work against ephemeral — and he corrects the picture instead: the precious stones are not gems but costly building stone such as marble, the hay is dried grass for filling chinks in walls, the stubble stalks with the ears cut off, used to thatch a roof. Robertson agrees, three durable materials against three perishable, a palace on the one hand and a mud hut on the other. Barnes widens it past teachers to any Christian and the hopes he cherishes. Chrysostom takes the coming fire and turns aside to the question all men ask, whether hell fire has any end, answering from the Lord's own words that their fire shall not be quenched. A chill comes over his hearers at it, he grants; but what else is he to do, when the charge is God's own?
13:
What the day is decides the passage, and Clarke takes it where nobody else will. He thinks it very probable that the Apostle refers to the approaching destruction of Jerusalem, the day being the punishment coming on that rebellious people and the fire pointing to the extreme rigour and totally destructive nature of that judgment — read so, he says, all the terms and metaphors appear clear and consistent. Barnes takes it for the day of judgment, which shall reveal the secrets of all hearts, though allowing that day may mean time in general, as we say that time will show. Robertson settles a grammatical question the others pass over: it is apparently the day that is subject of the verb, not the work and not the Lord; and the fire, a metaphor used already by the prophets and by John the Baptist, is not purgatorial but simple testing — a point for which he cites Ellicott by name. Ellicott is working the same ground from the preposition, preferring revealed in fire to by fire, and observing that the day of the Lord is always represented as bursting suddenly in light and fire; two verses later he says outright that the passage is metaphorical and not to be taken in a literal and physical sense, forgetting which the Roman divines have evolved from it the doctrine of purgatory. Calvin comes at it textually, collating the old English versions, suspecting that some words were added by way of explanation, and settling the sense from ordinary use: a day is when darkness is dispelled and truth brought to light. Wesley notices the tense — what faith beholds as certain and near is spoken of as already present. Gill turns it on the hearers, who shall see the deformity of a building at first so well laid, then piled with excellent materials, and at last covered in with trifling stuff.

On the work that stands, Clarke suspects an allusion to the purifying of vessels under the law, where what could bear the fire was purified by fire and the rest by water. Robertson notes that the condition is assumed as true, and reduces it to a question: when the fire has done its work, what is left? Calvin makes the failure one of judgment beforehand: those are fools who depend on man's estimation, since doctrines fly about unsettled and like empty bubbles glitter for a moment until thoroughly tested, so that all the applauses of the world must be reckoned as nothing. Ellicott gives the other man his picture: he escapes only by rushing through a conflagration, leaving everything that was his to be destroyed. Wesley is the gentlest, granting the reward to be a peculiar degree of glory and adding that some degree even the other will receive, having held the foundation, though he built on it through ignorance what would not abide the fire.

Whether the loss falls on the man or on his work is the last thing at issue, and Clarke states the alternative most fully. Some, he reports, refer the loss to the work and not the man, so that if any man's work be burned it shall suffer loss, nothing being left of it but the measure of truth it contained; Calvin registers the same alternative in terms of doctrine. Robertson keeps the loss on the man but bounds it: elsewhere the word covers the loss of the soul itself, but here there is no such total loss, for it is his work that is burned down — the preposition being perfective, so that we should say burned up in smoke. Barnes takes it as diminished standing, that he shall not be elevated to as high a rank as he otherwise would; Gill keeps it to the doctrine, rejected by the churches for not bearing the light and heat of the fire of God's word.
16:
Whose temple is meant is settled quickly. Barnes says it is the community of Christians, not the individual; Clarke reasons from the older case: as the congregation of Israel was the temple because God dwelt among them, so the whole Church at Corinth is — where God is, there is his temple. Robertson supplies the word: the sanctuary itself, not the sacred enclosure; and the Spirit makes his home in us, not in temples made with hands. Ellicott reads it as the completion of the figure, the Apostle moving from grand edifices to a building not only splendid but holy; and he hears a reproach in the opening, since do ye not know implies conduct only possible to the ignorant or forgetful. Calvin marks the change of address: having admonished the teachers he now turns to the pupils, the honour conferred being meant to make them the more reprehensible, that they may not prostitute themselves to the service of men.

The threat that follows turns on one verb, and Clarke says flatly that the clause is not consistently translated: the word is the same in both halves, so it should read, if any man destroy the temple of God, him will God destroy. Ellicott takes destroying as the opposite of building up, the teacher's work, and adds that the relative attaches to holy rather than temple — they are holy by the indwelling Spirit, and therefore are the temple. Robertson gives the warning a modern edge: it is a gross sin to be a church-wrecker, and there are actually a few preachers who leave ruin behind them like a tornado. Calvin specifies the profanation in view: men intruding themselves to bear rule in the Church in God's place, since once we are tinctured with the contrivances of men the temple is polluted as with filth. Gill names it philosophy and vain deceit. Two of them draw a line: Clarke distinguishes the erring man, who shall barely escape, from the obstinate opposer, who shall have judgment without mercy; Wesley points back over his shoulder, that this man shall not be saved at all, not even as through the fire.

Why the chapter turns at this point is answered two ways. Ellicott says the Apostle is returning to the subject he branched off from earlier, the magnifying of one teacher above another, to show that human wisdom is no ground for exalting the man who has it. Chrysostom reads a longer arc: having launched out before the proper time into his accusation of the fornicator and half opened it obscurely, so as to make that man's conscience quail, he hastens back to finish the battle with heathen wisdom, having had only a preliminary skirmish with the offender. On the self-deceit they are of one mind and differ only in force. Calvin says he here puts his finger on the true sore, the whole mischief having originated in their being wise in their own conceit; and hearers are addressed as well as teachers, since they lent an ear too readily to ambitious men, the simplicity of the gospel being insipid to so fastidious a taste. Henry prescribes humility as the remedy, warning that we are in great danger of deceiving ourselves when we have too high an opinion of human wisdom and arts. Barnes borrows a sentence from Grotius: all human philosophy repugnant to the gospel is but vain deceit. Clarke suspects a particular man behind the words, some troublesome individual who thought himself wiser than seven men that could render a reason; every church has more or less of these. Robertson diagnoses the mechanism: excited partisans can easily work themselves into a pious phrenzy and hypnotize themselves with their own supposed devotion to truth. Wesley states the cure in a line — let him become a fool such as the world accounts so, that he may become wise in God's account.
19:
Two of them take pains to keep the verse from condemning learning as such. Barnes says it does not mean that true wisdom is foolishness with God, nor that science and law, astronomy and medicine, are folly to him — God is the friend of truth on all subjects, and requires us to know his works. Calvin makes the same reservation and fixes the limit: natural perspicacity is a gift of God, and the liberal arts and the sciences are gifts of God, but they are confined within their own bounds and cannot penetrate his heavenly kingdom, so that they must occupy the place of handmaid and not of mistress. He also gives the argument its form, as one taken from opposites: we cannot be wise in the sight of God unless we are fools in the view of the world. Clarke reserves nothing. Whether it be the occult wisdom of the rabbins or the wire-drawn speculations of the Greeks, since folly is spending time and strength to no purpose, those may fitly be termed fools who acquire no saving knowledge by it — and is not this, he asks, the case with the major part of what is called philosophy even now? Has one soul been made wise unto salvation through it? Wesley finds the sting in the manner: they are taken not merely while they think they are acting wisely, but by their very wisdom, which is itself their snare.

The two quotations attract different kinds of notice. Ellicott observes that the first is from Job and the second from the Psalms, and adds the curiosity that this is the only allusion to that book anywhere in the New Testament save one, where the writer says his readers have heard rather than read of Job's patience — Robertson, counting quotations instead, making it two, here and in Romans, both varying from the Greek version. He also weighs the verb, an old word for grasping with the hand, more vivid than the Greek translators' and found nowhere else in the New Testament; and at the second quotation he notes that Paul changes the men of the Greek to the wise, in harmony with the Hebrew. Gill is interested in the joint rather than the words: the formula for citing a second passage answers to a rabbinic usage employed when the first proof does not settle the matter, the witnesses being Eliphaz confirmed by David. Barnes narrows that text: the affirmation is not about God's omniscience at large but about what he sees of the thoughts of the wise. Clarke widens it: what is said of the vanity of human knowledge is true of every kind of wisdom that does not lead immediately to God.

What the closing therefore looks back to is disputed, and Ellicott stands alone. It is not because of what has been mentioned, he says, but introduces what is about to be, the Apostle's enthusiasm over the privileges of Christians carrying him past what the argument required. Everyone else takes it as the conclusion of what precedes. Robertson calls it the inference from the self-conceit just condemned, glorying in party being inconsistent with glorying in the Lord. Calvin pushes it furthest: nothing being more vain than man, there is little security in leaning on an evanescent shadow, and any supremacy of man by which the glory of Christ is impaired involves sacrilege. Henry describes the fault: forgetting that ministers are men, paying them deference due only to God, setting them at the head of parties, servilely following their dictates. Gill says the same of the false teachers, whose eloquence so ensnared them that they called them masters and pinned their faith on their sleeve. Clarke and Wesley turn to the compensation: he that has God for his portion has all that can make him happy, and the ministers are not lords but servants.
22:
The list itself is read as an argument. Wesley notices the shape of it: the leap from Peter to the world greatly enlarges the thought and argues a kind of impatience of enumerating the rest, so that every one in the world, however excellent, is their servant too. Contend no more about these little things, he ends, but be united in love as ye are in blessings. Clarke turns the possession round: the ministers of the Church are appointed for the hearers and not the hearers for the ministers, just as the ordinances of grace are for them and not they for the ordinances. He also narrows one item, since the word rendered world means rather the inhabitants of it than what we commonly understand by the world itself, as in the complaint that the world is gone after him. Barnes states the doctrine: whatever comes of any preacher's piety and labours is theirs, one being as much entitled as another, so that ministers belong to the church, which enjoys their learning and zeal in common. Gill puts it in terms of gifts, received for them and bestowed not so much for the ministers' own use as for the good of others. Robertson attends to what is not there. Every word in these two verses stands without the article, though none is indefinite: proper names do not need it, nor do words for single objects like world, life and death, and the article must not be thought of as omitted. The wealth of the Christian, he concludes, takes in all things, all leaders, past, present and future, Christ and God, with no room in it for partisan wrangling. Calvin sets their station by the one place that cannot be shared: it must not detract in any degree from the authority of Christ, sole Master of the Church, alone worthy to be heard and alone commended by the Father with the words hear ye him.

Why the sentence does not stop at ye are Christ's gets two answers. Ellicott offers the sharper. The last clause is probably added not only as the climax of the ascent up which the whole passage has been going, but to prevent the party who called themselves by the name of Christ from arrogating anything out of the preceding words, had it ended there. Calvin answers from the other end: it is added to show that the sum of our felicity consists in union with God the chief good, accomplished when we are gathered under the Master he has set over us. On what the clause means they are unanimous, and each guards it. All four refer it to the mediatorial office. Calvin adds that the subjection relates to Christ's humanity, since by taking our flesh he assumed the form of a servant; Clarke, that in his human nature he is as much the property of God as any other man, and as mediator must in a certain way be considered inferior, while in his own essential nature there is no inequality; Wesley reduces it to a line, that as Mediator he refers all his services to his Father's glory. Ellicott adds that in that early age there was no danger of the words being misunderstood as implying any want of absolute identity between the Son and the Father in his divine nature, as some have endeavoured to misunderstand them since. Gill traces the title through its grounds — not by creation only, as all men are Christ's, but by the Father's gift, the purchase of his blood, a voluntary surrender, profession and possession — and pushes the mutual property to its hardest case, that even their worst things are his, their sins laid on him by imputation. Barnes keeps the argument in view: they belong to Christ and he to God, and are bound therefore not to devote themselves to a man.
